barCharacter: Liam de Lioncourt: the over-formal, self-important aesthete whose elevated register is the joke and whose secret earnestness keeps betraying him. Closest comic job to Quill (florid poseur, secret failure). Liam has only about eight spoken lines in the corpus, so his set is filled out with narration about him and player lines aimed at him.

ours: Dash is as promising as a tulip in sixteen thirty-seven. Much admired. Briefly. Then worth an onion.
I challenged the little red clerk who underlineth my words to a duel. He underlined the challenge.
Choose me, and all thy virtues I shall prove. In sixteen hundred, that rhymed with love.
She was a milkmaid in a pastoral. She left the pastoral. I am still standing in the field.
I have fought forty duels. I have lost none. Thou art welcome to inspect my wounds.
Thy coldness wounds me like a musket ball. Slowly, inaccurately, and with great noise.
Prince, a true nobleman never asketh for a processing fee. He asketh for a dowry. Learn thy trade.
My muse laughed at my ruff. I have challenged the ruff to a duel. The ruff is winning.
These three would love thee for a season. I shall make thee immortal. Bound in calfskin.
Nav is a ferryman with no boat and no river, only opinions about left turns.
I challenged {rival} to a duel. {rival} accepted. Nobody hath ever accepted. I am terrified.
Fie. That line was stale when the plague was fresh.
bar: Maybe doing a 180 degree spin from cliches is good, but embracing cliches is like... making a 360 degree spin from them! So disruptive!
You! Save me from the consequences of my actions! Suggest an idea that lives up to my own hype!
Ugh- I have no reason to care about this, but suddenly it's all I care about! Someone stop this madness!
Please, friend, help me find an unpopular band to worship until pop culture inevitably ruins it.
Yes, we have indeed encountered a culinary block. Perhaps you can suggest something appropriately artistic?
But I was sighing deeply because I couldn't help but think: supposing I were to actually acquire such a machine, I wonder...where in time would I go?
What kind of status could I post that would be idiot-proof?
Narrator: a hipster vampire whose stand-offish demeanor hid that he was truly a lovable dork.
Narrator: Liam vanishes in a cloud of mist and angst.
Narrator: Later, you see Liam beaming to himself. Liam? Beaming?
Player option: 3.85 billion BC, so you can be into existing before it was cool.
Player option: Well, I guess I'll be going then, because there's no way anyone could ever be as cool as Liam.
headToHead.voiceJudgement: Cover the names and Quill is identified instantly, but by diction (thee, -eth, ruff, duel), not by sentence shape. Strip the archaic inflections and most of his twelve best are the house cadence every bot in this cast uses: a short declarative, a fragment, a fragment-turn ('Much admired. Briefly. Then worth an onion.' / 'I have lost none. Thou art welcome to inspect my wounds.'). That cadence is the opposite of his written flaw, 'cannot say one thing plainly'; he is written as the plainest, most clipped speaker in the cast, in costume. Liam is identified by syntax: formal subordinate clauses spent on trivia ('supposing I were to actually acquire such a machine', 'encountered a culinary block') and a plea at the end. But two of Liam's seven spoken lines ('What kind of status...', 'Ugh- I have no reason to care...') could be Vera or Polly. Net: a tie, Quill on diction, Liam on shape.
headToHead.constructionJudgement: Quill's top twelve are tight: most land on their last two to four words ('Bound in calfskin.', 'Then worth an onion.', 'He underlined the challenge.', 'The ruff is winning.'), and none explains itself. Liam's lines are looser and longer (27 words for the time-machine setup), but they do what Quill's rarely do: each states a want and hands the player a problem, and the 180/360 line makes him wrong in the act of sounding clever, which is a self-betrayal in one sentence. Quill's twelve all run the same three-beat cadence, so by the sixth the rhythm is predictable even when the words are good. On economy ours wins, on variety and on want the bar wins; called a tie.
headToHead.quotableJudgement: The 360-degree spin and 'Save me from the consequences of my actions! Suggest an idea that lives up to my own hype!' are the lines people actually repeat, because the character's status move and his self-betrayal are the same sentence. Quill has three genuine clips (the tulip, the little red clerk, prove/love) but they are clever about history and spelling rather than about Quill; the clip is the wordplay, not the man. A viewer quotes Liam to describe a person; a viewer would quote Quill to show a joke. Bar wins.

templates: Duel / glove / 'at dawn': 18 of 112 lines carry a challenge, a glove or a dawn; 'at dawn' or 'Dawn.' closes six of them. The best instances (forty duels, the little red clerk, the ruff is winning, {rival} accepted) are left out of the generic count; the other fourteen add nothing.
'In my century' / 'in my day we called that' / 'we called them': 12 lines. The anachronism tag is the bank's main crutch and appears in roasts, answers, confessions, one-on-ones and the lose line.

The unfinished last line (his secret): 10 lines across openers, confessions, twists, closes and the win. A runner is right; ten variants on a 112-line bank is too many, and three of them state it rather than show it.
'A simple yes costs a sonnet': q-worst-habit, worst-trait, apology, q-fight and the 'speak plainly' one-on-one opener, 5 lines on one premise.
Ruff as prop: 6 lines. Leech as prop: 3 lines.
Self-correction tag ('Correction: my ruff.', 'No, reverse it.', 'Bring two.', 'Twice, so far.', 'Eight and a bit.', 'Briefly.'): 6 lines.

House staccato: 'Statement. Fragment. Fragment-turn.' is the shape of well over half the bank ('Wed. A cottage. A son named Spondee.', 'Lost. Very well.', 'A smile. I nearly wrote a last line. Nearly.', 'Ahem. No.'), and it is the same cadence the other suitors use.
ruleBreaks: No line over its limit (openers max 12/12, jabs max 10/10, everything else max 20/20; the motherboard and comma lines sit exactly on 20). No em dashes, no emoji, no asterisks or stage directions, no real person or brand, nothing beyond PG-13 (a glove across the face and pistols at dawn are fine).
Contraction, which the persona forbids: 'How dar'st thou speak such prose in front of me.'

Modern idiom or slang in a bot told 'never use slang': 'I have it handled' ('Whoever laughed at my ruff...'), 'Get comfortable.' ('Thou art right, and I yield...'), 'A feature:' ('I cannot say anything plainly...'), and 'I talk like a dead man' dropping the -eth form in the same line as 'talketh'.

Renaming rule broken: he says the real modern word instead of renaming it: 'Honoured motherboard...' and 'Gracious motherboard...' (the twist hands him the word; he should rename it), 'machine' three times ('{rival} talketh like a machine...', 'When they speak, a machine speaketh...', 'Thou art older than these machines...'), 'My logs show...'.
Therapy-adjacent: 'I do not need to be loved. I need someone to stay until the last line. Nobody stays.' The first sentence is the therapy register; the last-line image would work without it.
Stock romance filler: 'old flame' ('Thou hadst thy chapter, old flame...') and 'Thou hast rendered me speechless...'.

Lists in disguise: 'I own three quills, a ruff, and a sonnet worth forty ducats...', 'Wed. A cottage. A son named Spondee...', 'Brock is strong as an ox, loyal as an ox, and, alas, conversational as an ox.'

The persona's signature move is nearly missing: 'Slighted, answer in one line of iambic pentameter' appears in only four lines ('O suitor, thou dost bore me unto death', 'Pick me, for I am constant as the tide', 'Choose me, and all thy virtues I shall prove', 'How dar'st thou speak such prose in front of me'), and none of the three closeCold lines, where he has just been slighted, is in verse.
Too nice for a star with standards: not applicable, this bank has no star reactions or cuts.
biggestGap: Quill is written as the most clipped, plain-spoken deadpan in the cast wearing thee-and-thou, when his flaw is that he cannot say one thing plainly: make the flaw the sentence shape, so most lines are one long overdressed sentence (an O-apostrophe, an inversion, a dead simile, a subordinate clause spent on something trivial, as Liam spends his) that strains toward the point and then either collapses into two plain words or stops one word short, and every slight is answered in a single strict pentameter line instead of a quip.

notes: Bar file read in full (refs/writing/monster-prom-lines.md, including the voice section); charm-notes.md read. 112 lines in the bank; 54 flagged generic or templated (48.2%). A line is flagged if any test catches it; strong lines that share a template but turn on something specific (forty duels, the little red clerk, the ruff is winning, {rival} accepted, prove/love, the tulip, Frost's grandmother) are left out of the count, so the template totals run higher than their share of genericLines. Construction faults outside the four tests: the Tilly roast's simile breaks ('the way a church bell saith noon. Constantly' : a bell says noon once a day); the leech opener's simile does not describe eyes; 'When they speak... sixteen hundred and eleven speaketh' needs the viewer to know 1611. MP's shared engine (one want per line, handed to the listener as a demand) is almost absent: Quill's lines describe him but rarely ask the star for anything; 'Do not skip. Please. Line one.' is the one that does, and it is one of his best. Rival overlap: Prince already owns lavish-formal address and Maximilian owns 'I shall have that...' courtesy, so Quill's 'I shall have it set to harpsichord by morning' and 'Ring every bell in the parish' sit in their lane; Quill's register should be verse and archaism, not formality. Protect the dead-simile engine (tulip, musket ball, sedan chair, ferryman) and the renamings (little red clerk, glowing hand-mirror, invisible postman, cupboard); they are what no other bot can say.
